---
title: "What this grammar does not do"
---

A tool's marketing lists what it has. A manual you can trust also lists what
it lacks, so here are both directions, measured against dplyr and pandas as
of god 0.0.1, in August 2026. The first list will shrink as the vocabulary
grows under its laws; the honest way to read it today is as the price of the
small grammar the rest of this book sells.

## The gaps, and their exits

Each row names the gap and the exit. The exit is always real: `show_as`
renders your pipeline in the host tool, and you finish the last step there,
in code you can read because you watched it being written.

| the gap | what to do today |
|---|---|
| Rolling and sliding windows (a seven-day average) | `show_as` the pipeline, add the rolling step in the host |
| Regular expressions | `starts`, `ends`, `contains`, `replace_text`, `split_text` cover the common cases; regex stays in the host |
| Arbitrary functions in a cell (`apply`, a lambda) | the scalar vocabulary is closed; the host is the place for host code |
| List-columns and nested data | god reads a table of plain values; nest and unnest in the host |
| `widen` with several value columns at once | one `name`, one `value` per `widen`; run it twice and `join` |
| Joins on anything but equality (ranges, nearest) | equality joins only; inequality joins in the host |
| Random sampling | refused by the settled-answer law; sample in the host, then hand the table over |
| The long aggregate shelf (variance, quantiles, weighted means, mode) | nine aggregations; the rest via `show_as` |
| Row-wise aggregates across many columns | [one value per column](../chapters/one-value-per-column.qmd) sweeps a calculation across columns one at a time; a row-wise `sum` of fifty columns is the host's |
| Window frames (`ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING`) | `running_total`, `previous`, `following` are the whole windowed family today |

Two of these are refusals with a law behind them rather than absences, and
the distinction matters: sampling and arbitrary functions will not arrive
later, because the settled-answer law and the closed-cell law refuse them on
purpose. The others are ordinary absences, candidates like any other word,
waiting on the growth test every candidate faces.

## What god does that they do not

- **One vocabulary in two languages.** The same sentence, spelled the same,
  in R and in Python, with the differences confined to the pipe and the
  column. Nothing else on this list matters more.
- **The whole pipeline checked before anything runs.** A six-step pipeline
  with a typo in step five costs nothing and names step five.
- **Refusals written by one voice, carrying their repair.** Not the engine's
  stack trace, whichever engine it was.
- **Assumptions printed back.** Where the grammar decided something you did
  not say, the decision is on the page.
- **`matching`: the join that cannot multiply rows**, so the question "has a
  partner?" is a different word from the act "bring columns in".
- **The same sentence wherever it goes.** DuckDB and Spark execute it; dplyr,
  pandas, polars and PySpark receive it as readable code; a warehouse runs
  it where the table lives.
- **An exit that is part of the design.** Leaving god costs one `show_as`
  per pipeline, which is the strongest promise a small tool can make and
  the reason its smallness is safe to depend on.

## How this list stays honest

Both halves of this page age, in opposite directions. The plan is the same
as for every claim in this book: dated, and corrected in public when it
drifts. If you catch either list out of date, that is a defect worth an
issue, exactly like a refusal that stopped refusing.
